title: The Rime of the Ancient Mariner
author: Samuel Taylor Coleridge
written: Planned on a walk in November 1797 and finished by March 1798; revised at intervals until 1834
setting: The road outside a wedding feast, and inside the tale a voyage from a home harbour south to the polar ice, north again into a becalmed tropical sea, and home
lengthNote: 625 lines in seven parts, mostly four-line ballad stanzas that stretch to five, six and once nine lines when the tale needs room
openingLine: It is an ancient Mariner, And he stoppeth one of three.
summary: An old sailor stops a man on his way into a wedding and will not let him go. The story he tells has a crime in it that takes two lines and no explanation, a punishment that falls hardest on two hundred men who did not commit it, and a release that arrives while he is not trying for it. It ends with a neat moral about loving all creatures, spoken by a man who is still, decades later, compelled to seize strangers, and heard by one who goes home stunned and skips the party.
referenceStyle: part — the source text prints the seven parts without line numbers, so quotations are placed by part alone

sourceText.label: Project Gutenberg text of The Rime of the Ancient Mariner (eBook #151)
sourceText.note: Quotations follow this transcription of the late text in seven parts, the version Coleridge settled in his collected editions and the one the Astor edition prints as the 1834 text. It is the verse only: it carries no line numbers, and it omits the Latin epigraph and the prose marginal gloss added in 1817, so the gloss is described here but never quoted. The spelling is the revised spelling, not the mock-antique 'Ancyent Marinere' of 1798, and readers comparing the first printing will find stanzas there that Coleridge later cut.

atAGlance.label: First published
atAGlance.note: Anonymously, as the opening poem of Lyrical Ballads, under the title 'The Rime of the Ancyent Marinere'.

atAGlance.label: Marginal gloss added
atAGlance.note: In Sibylline Leaves, where the poem first appeared under Coleridge's own name, with a Latin epigraph in place of the old prose Argument.

atAGlance.label: Text followed here
atAGlance.note: The last version Coleridge saw through the press, in the year of his death.

atAGlance.label: Form
atAGlance.note: Alternating four- and three-stress lines, rhymed on the short lines, with internal rhyme in many of the long ones.

structure.label: Part I
structure.title: The guest is stopped, the ship goes south, the bird is shot
structure.summary: The Mariner picks one man out of three and holds him first by the hand and then, more effectively, by the eye. The voyage runs south past the equator into a storm and then into ice, where an albatross arrives, is fed, and seems to bring a wind. The part ends on the Wedding-Guest's alarm at the teller's face and the flat confession it draws out.

structure.label: Part II
structure.title: The crew change their minds, and the wind stops
structure.summary: The shipmates first blame the Mariner for killing the bird of good luck and then, when the fog lifts, approve the killing, which makes them parties to it. The ship bursts into an unvisited sea and is becalmed under a small, bloody sun. Thirst sets in, the water seems to rot and burn, and the crew hang the dead bird round his neck.

structure.label: Part III
structure.title: The spectre-bark and the game of dice
structure.summary: A sail appears, and the Mariner has to bite his own arm and drink the blood before he can call out. The ship that comes moves without wind, shows the sun through its ribs, and carries Death and a woman named Life-in-Death, who dice for the crew. She wins the Mariner; night falls at one stride; and two hundred men drop dead one by one, each cursing him with a look.

structure.label: Part IV
structure.title: Seven days alone, and the water-snakes
structure.summary: The Wedding-Guest fears he is talking to a ghost and is told, not very comfortingly, that this body did not drop. Alone among the corpses, unable to pray or die, the Mariner watches the moon go up and then the water-snakes moving in the ship's shadow. He blesses them without meaning to, finds he can pray, and the albatross falls from his neck into the sea.

structure.label: Part V
structure.title: Rain, the dead men working, and two voices
structure.summary: Sleep and rain come. The ship moves without a breeze, worked by the bodies of the crew, which at dawn give out sweet sounds that fly to the sun and back. The spirit from the land of mist and snow carries the ship as far as the equator and lets go; the Mariner faints, and overhears two voices agreeing that he has done penance and will do more.

structure.label: Part VI
structure.title: The trance, the curse again, and the home harbour
structure.summary: The voices explain how the ship is being driven while he lies in a trance. He wakes to find the dead men still staring, until the spell snaps and a private wind carries him home to the same lighthouse, hill and kirk he left. Seraphs stand on the corpses as signal lights, and a boat puts out with the Pilot, his boy and the Hermit.

structure.label: Part VII
structure.title: The ship sinks, the Hermit asks, and the telling begins
structure.summary: The ship goes down like lead as the boat reaches it. The rescued Mariner terrifies all three rescuers, begs the Hermit to shrieve him, and is asked instead what kind of man he is, which wrenches the tale out of him for the first time. He explains that the agony comes back at uncertain hours, delivers his moral, and goes; the Wedding-Guest turns away from the feast.

characters.name: The Ancient Mariner
characters.role: Teller of the tale and its only survivor
characters.summary: He has no name, no rank and no stated reason for the one act that defines him, and the poem is careful to keep it that way. What he has instead is an eye that fixes listeners, a body that frightens everybody who sees it, and a story he cannot choose not to tell. He is often read as a penitent who has learned his lesson; the verse also shows a man whose punishment has simply changed its form, from thirst to narration.
characters.clue: He shoots a bird with a crossbow, wears it round his neck, and years later knows on sight the face of the next man who must hear about it.

relationships.label: cursed by, and works beside the bodies of

characters.name: The Wedding-Guest
characters.role: The listener, next of kin to the bridegroom
characters.summary: He is the reader's stand-in and the poem's control experiment: a cheerful man with somewhere to be, who protests, beats his breast at the sound of the bassoon, and still cannot get up. His interruptions mark the moments at which the tale becomes hardest to bear, and his last state is the only evidence the poem offers of what the story does to a person who hears it.
characters.clue: He sits on a stone within earshot of the music, twice says that he is afraid of the man talking to him, and never goes in.

characters.name: The Albatross
characters.role: The bird that comes through the fog
characters.summary: In the verse it does very little: it arrives, eats what the sailors give it, circles the ship and perches on the rigging for nine evenings. Everything else is put on it by other people. The crew hail it as if it were a Christian soul, then decide it brought the wind, then decide it brought the fog; a spirit is said to have loved it; and it ends as a weight hung where a cross should be.
characters.clue: It comes to the sailors' call for food or play, and the last thing said about it is that it sank like lead.

characters.name: The crew
characters.role: Two hundred shipmates, living and then dead
characters.summary: They judge the killing by its results, condemning it while the luck holds and praising it when the sun comes out, and the poem makes that change of mind their share in the crime. Their deaths are nonetheless out of all proportion, which is one of the difficulties the poem leaves standing. After death they are its strangest image: bodies that work the ropes in silence, among them the Mariner's own nephew, and whose open eyes go on cursing him.
characters.clue: They say he was wrong to kill the bird, then right, then hang it round his neck, and later pull on the same rope as him without a word.

characters.name: Life-in-Death
characters.summary: She is painted in the colours of a ballad beauty, red lips and yellow hair, with one detail wrong: skin as white as leprosy. Her name, which Coleridge added in revision, describes the sentence she wins for the Mariner, which is not to die. She speaks one line, of triumph at a throw of the dice, and that line is the nearest thing the poem offers to an account of how its justice is decided.
characters.clue: She whistles three times when she wins, and what she has won is a man who will spend seven days wishing he could die.

characters.name: Death
characters.role: Her companion on the skeleton ship
characters.summary: He is hardly described at all in the late text, which cut the grisly portrait that the 1798 version gave him, so that he survives mainly as a question the Mariner asks on seeing the ship. He loses the throw for the Mariner and, by implication, takes the rest: two hundred men, who go down with a thump while the poem looks the other way at the rising moon.
characters.clue: He is the woman's mate, he plays dice on a ship with no planking, and he is never heard to speak.

characters.name: The Polar Spirit
characters.role: The spirit from the land of mist and snow
characters.summary: The verse never names him; the title comes from the prose gloss of 1817. He is known only at second hand, through the crew's dreams, which place him nine fathoms under the keel, and through two voices who say he loved the bird. He both avenges the albatross and, under orders the poem does not explain, carries the ship north as far as the equator, where his reach ends and the ship jolts free.
characters.clue: He follows nine fathom deep, is reported by dreamers and overheard voices, and is never seen by anybody.

characters.name: The Hermit
characters.role: The holy man of the wood by the harbour
characters.summary: He is the poem's picture of religion lived at ease in nature: he sings hymns of his own making, kneels on a mossy oak-stump and likes talking to sailors. The Mariner expects him to wash the blood away. What the Hermit actually does is cross himself and ask a question, and the answer to that question is the first telling of the tale, so that the confessor starts the compulsion rather than ending it.
characters.clue: He compares the ship's sails to dead leaves in his forest brook, urges the boat on when the Pilot is afraid, and can scarcely stand when he steps ashore.

relationships.label: questions, and so becomes the first listener of

characters.name: The Pilot
characters.role: The harbour pilot who rows out to the ship
characters.summary: An ordinary working man brought to the edge of the supernatural, he serves to measure how the Mariner now looks to the world he has come back to. He thinks the ship fiendish before he reaches it, and when the drowned-looking body in his boat moves its lips he shrieks and falls down in a fit.
characters.clue: He says he is afraid, is told to push on, and collapses when the man he has rescued tries to speak.

characters.name: The Pilot's boy
characters.role: The lad in the rescue boat
characters.summary: He has the poem's most disturbing line after the shooting itself. Watching the Mariner take the oars, he laughs long and loud with his eyes going to and fro, and says what the adults are too frightened or too pious to say. The Mariner adds, in passing and in the present tense, that the boy is mad now, which is the cost of the homecoming to somebody who only came out in a boat.
characters.clue: He laughs, names the Devil as the oarsman, and is mentioned once more as one who now goes crazy.

themes.name: A crime without a motive
themes.summary: The shooting is given one clause and no reason, and the poem never goes back to supply one. That omission is the centre of the work: guilt here is not the consequence of a bad intention that can be examined and repented, but a fact that attaches to a man and has to be carried, first as a dead bird and then as a story. The crew's guilt is different in kind, a matter of approving after the event, and is punished more severely.
themes.development: Stated in a line at the end of Part I, made visible as a burden at the end of Part II, lifted from the neck in Part IV, and shown in Part VII to have moved inwards, where it returns at uncertain hours.

themes.name: The living world, slimy and beautiful
themes.summary: The same sea creatures appear twice. In Part II they are slimy things crawling on a rotting sea, and in Part IV they are water-snakes in blue, green and velvet black, shedding light as they rear. Nothing about them has altered except the way they are looked at, and the poem locates the Mariner's release in that change of looking. The sun in this poem tends to preside over suffering and the moon over relief, a pattern too consistent to be accidental and too loose to be a code.
themes.development: From the bird treated as a guest and then as a target in Part I, through disgust in Part II and unwilled love in Part IV, to the closing claim that prayer and the love of creatures are one act.

themes.name: Alone on a wide wide sea
themes.summary: The Mariner's punishment is solitude in company: two hundred bodies on deck, every one with its eyes open, and nobody to speak to. The poem treats loneliness as a spiritual condition as well as a physical one, since at its worst he cannot pray either. His later longing is touchingly modest. He does not ask for the wedding feast, only to walk to church in a crowd.
themes.development: Introduced when the ship breaks into a sea nobody has entered, brought to its extreme in Part IV, and carried home in Part VII, where the man who praises company passes like night from land to land and belongs nowhere.

themes.name: Penance without an end
themes.summary: The poem borrows the vocabulary of confession, with its shrieving and penance and a hermit to hear it, and then declines to complete the sacrament. The albatross falls off, the curse is snapped and the ship comes home, yet a voice has already said that more penance is to come, and the Hermit gives a question instead of absolution. Release in this poem is real but partial, and it is never declared finished.
themes.development: First relief in Part IV; the verdict of the second voice at the end of Part V; the hope of being shrieved at the end of Part VI; and in Part VII the discovery that telling the tale frees him only until the next time.

themes.name: The tale that has to be told
themes.summary: The poem is about being told a story as much as about the story. It opens on a listener being stopped and closes on what listening has done to him, and in between the teller explains that he does not choose his moments or his audience. Storytelling is therefore shown from both ends as something undergone. It is a penance for the speaker and, the last stanza suggests, an injury as well as an education for the hearer.
themes.development: The frame is set in the first stanza, interrupts the voyage at its most frightening points in Parts I, IV and V, and takes over completely in Part VII, where the origin and mechanism of the compulsion are finally given.

themes.name: Prayer, chance and an unsteady providence
themes.summary: The Mariner's world is thick with Christian reference, from vespers and the Virgin to the holy rood and guardian saints, and he reads his rescue as grace. But the poem also shows his fate settled by a throw of dice between two spectres, and a sea so lonely that God himself scarcely seemed to be there. It holds both pictures without choosing, which is why it has been read as an orthodox parable and as a nightmare with a parable pinned to it.
themes.development: The bird is greeted in God's name in Part I; the dice fall in Part III; prayer fails and then succeeds in Part IV; and Part VII ends with a creed whose comfort the listener's condition does not quite confirm.

techniques.name: Frame narrative
techniques.definition: A story told inside another story, so that every account reaches the reader through somebody with an interest in it.
techniques.inThisBook: The voyage is enclosed in an encounter on a road outside a wedding. The frame breaks in whenever the Wedding-Guest can bear no more, and it supplies the ending: the last two stanzas are about him, not the Mariner. After 1817 a second frame, the prose gloss in the margin, tells the story again in a confident scholarly voice that knows more, or claims to, than the verse does.

techniques.name: Ballad stanza
techniques.definition: A four-line stanza alternating four-stress and three-stress lines, rhymed on the second and fourth, inherited from traditional sung narrative.
techniques.inThisBook: Coleridge keeps the old measure for speed and plainness and then breaks it for effect. When the storm drives the ship, when the spectre-bark closes in, when the fiend treads behind on the lonesome road, the stanza swells to five or six lines, so that the reader waits longer than expected for the rhyme to close.

techniques.name: Internal rhyme
techniques.definition: A rhyme between the middle and the end of a single line, rather than between line-endings.
techniques.inThisBook: Many of the long lines chime at the half-way point: guests met and feast set, the ice that did split with a thunder-fit, the first that ever burst. The effect is a gallop in the passages of motion and, in the becalmed passages, a kind of locked echo in which the line seems unable to get away from itself.

techniques.name: Refrain
techniques.definition: A phrase brought back at intervals, so that its meaning shifts with what has happened since.
techniques.inThisBook: Repetition works at every scale, from doubled words within a line to whole stanzas that return altered. The sun that came up upon the left in Part I rises upon the right in Part II, which is how the poem says the ship has rounded the ice; the lighthouse, hill and kirk of the departure come back in reverse order at the homecoming; and the word 'alone' is struck five times in two lines.

techniques.name: Archaism
techniques.definition: The deliberate use of words and forms already old-fashioned when the work was written.
techniques.inThisBook: Words such as eftsoons, swound, gramercy, clomb and I wist give the poem the air of something found rather than written, and the 1798 text went further with antique spelling throughout. Coleridge pared much of this away in revision, but kept enough that the tale seems to come from no particular century, which suits a teller who is himself out of time.

techniques.name: Simile
techniques.definition: A comparison made explicit with 'like' or 'as', so that the two things are held side by side rather than fused.
techniques.inThisBook: The similes repeatedly reach away from the sea towards the land the Mariner has lost: a hidden brook in the leafy month of June, a meadow-gale of spring, April hoar-frost. Others turn the ship into a picture or a prison, as with the painted ship and the sun peering through a dungeon-grate. The most famous of them, the man on the lonesome road, describes fear by refusing to look at its cause.

techniques.name: The unstable symbol
techniques.definition: An object placed at the centre of a work whose meaning is never settled by it.
techniques.inThisBook: The albatross is hailed as a soul, credited with the wind, blamed for the fog, hung in the place of a cross and mourned by a spirit, all by characters with reasons of their own. The verse itself never says what the bird means, only what is done with it. Readings that make it Christ, nature, the imagination or an innocent stranger are all continuing the crew's habit of deciding after the fact.

quotations.text: It is an ancient Mariner, And he stoppeth one of three.
quotations.context: The opening couplet, before anybody has spoken.
quotations.analysis: 'It is', not 'there was': the present tense puts the Mariner in front of us as something encountered, almost as a thing, and the same tense will return at the end when we learn he is still doing this. 'One of three' is never explained. Two men walk on into the wedding, and the poem's first act is a selection without a stated reason, which prepares for a story built on another.

quotations.text: He holds him with his glittering eye-- The Wedding-Guest stood still, And listens like a three years child: The Mariner hath his will.
quotations.context: The Mariner has been told to take his hand away, and does; this is what he uses instead.
quotations.analysis: The hand fails and the eye succeeds, so the hold is not physical and the guest's consent is not asked. Comparing a grown man to a three years child makes listening a return to helplessness. 'Hath his will' is a phrase of mastery, and it sits oddly on a man we later learn has no will of his own in the matter, since the tale compels him as he compels the guest.

quotations.text: As if it had been a Christian soul, We hailed it in God's name.
quotations.context: The albatross comes through the fog to a ship surrounded by ice, where no living thing has been seen.
quotations.analysis: The sailors greet the first creature they have met in the ice as one greets a person, and the 'as if' keeps the comparison honest: nobody claims the bird is a soul. What the line establishes is hospitality. The bird is received as a guest, fed, and called to, so that the shooting nine evenings later is a breach of welcome before it is anything more mysterious.

quotations.text: "God save thee, ancient Mariner! From the fiends, that plague thee thus!-- Why look'st thou so?"--With my cross-bow I shot the ALBATROSS.
quotations.context: The Wedding-Guest breaks in at the sight of the Mariner's face, and the answer closes the first part.
quotations.analysis: The confession is made in reply to a question about his expression, not about his conduct, and it answers 'why' with 'what'. The instrument comes first and the verb is the plainest available. There is no because, then or afterwards. Placing the act at the very end of the part, after a stanza of moonshine and vespers, gives it the abruptness of the thing itself, and the capitals are the text's way of letting the word ring.

quotations.text: For all averred, I had killed the bird That made the breeze to blow.
quotations.context: The first verdict of the shipmates, while the wind still holds but the bird no longer follows.
quotations.analysis: 'Averred' is a word for sworn testimony, and the crew use it twice, a stanza apart, for opposite findings: that he killed the bird that brought the breeze, and that he killed the bird that brought the fog. Their morality is a weather report. The poem quietly treats the second verdict as the fatal one, since approving the act afterwards is the only thing the two hundred ever do to deserve what follows.

quotations.text: We were the first that ever burst Into that silent sea.
quotations.context: The ship, running north with a fair wind, enters waters no ship has sailed.
quotations.analysis: For two lines the poem sounds like the voyage narratives Coleridge had been reading, with the explorer's boast of priority. 'Burst' is a violent verb for an arrival, and it rhymes inside the line with 'first', so that discovery and intrusion are heard as one sound. The silence they break into is about to become their own: in the next stanza the wind drops, and they speak only to hear something.

quotations.text: Day after day, day after day, We stuck, nor breath nor motion; As idle as a painted ship Upon a painted ocean.
quotations.context: The ship is becalmed under a copper sky.
quotations.analysis: The first line does what it describes, repeating itself because nothing has happened to report. The simile is stranger than it looks. A becalmed ship is compared to a picture of a ship, which is to say to art, and the comparison is a complaint: to be a painting is to be without breath. In a poem so concerned with what it is to be fixed by a tale, the image of people trapped in a representation is not idle.

quotations.text: Water, water, every where, And all the boards did shrink; Water, water, every where, Nor any drop to drink.
quotations.context: Thirst begins among the becalmed crew.
quotations.analysis: The line most people know is usually misquoted, and the true second line is the more exact observation: salt water and sun are shrinking the planks of the ship itself, so the sea surrounds them and is also pulling their shelter apart. The stanza is a riddle of abundance as deprivation. It prepares for Part IV, where the Mariner is surrounded by life and cannot be part of it until he sees it differently.

quotations.text: Instead of the cross, the Albatross About my neck was hung.
quotations.context: The close of Part II: the crew, too parched to speak, express themselves in an act.
quotations.analysis: The rhyme of 'cross' and 'Albatross' falls inside one line and makes the substitution audible. The passive voice matters: he does not take the bird up, it is hung on him by men who have themselves approved the killing, which makes this a scapegoating as much as a penance. Whether the bird is thereby likened to Christ, or whether the emblem of forgiveness has simply been replaced by the evidence of the offence, the line declines to say.

quotations.text: I bit my arm, I sucked the blood, And cried, A sail! a sail!
quotations.context: A shape has been sighted, and nobody on board has moisture enough in his mouth to call out.
quotations.analysis: To speak at all he has to drink from himself, and the poem sets down the fact in two short clauses without comment. It is the first time speech costs the Mariner blood, and it will not be the last: every later telling of the tale is wrung from him by a bodily agony. The hope he pays for so dearly is also mistaken, since the sail is the spectre-bark.

quotations.text: Her lips were red, her looks were free, Her locks were yellow as gold: Her skin was as white as leprosy, The Night-Mare LIFE-IN-DEATH was she, Who thicks man's blood with cold.
quotations.context: The Mariner sees the two figures on the skeleton ship as it comes alongside.
quotations.analysis: The first two lines are the stock portrait of a ballad heroine, and the third spoils it with a single noun. Red, gold and white are the colours of beauty, and white is also the colour of the disease, so the portrait turns on its own palette. The stanza runs to five lines because the name needs a line to itself. 'Thicks' is used as a verb, an old usage that makes the cold seem to act inside the listener's own veins.

quotations.text: The game is done! I've won! I've won!
quotations.context: Death and Life-in-Death have been casting dice on the deck of the hulk; this is her cry.
quotations.analysis: The poem's only glimpse of how sentences are passed in its universe is a game of chance, and the winner's glee is a child's. If the Mariner's survival is a prize in a dice game, then the moral economy of sin, penance and grace that he later describes has a rival explanation underneath it. The gloss of 1817 tidies this scene into a judgement; the verse leaves it as a throw.

quotations.text: And every soul, it passed me by, Like the whizz of my CROSS-BOW!
quotations.context: The last lines of Part III: two hundred men have dropped dead, and their souls leave their bodies.
quotations.analysis: Each part of the poem so far has ended on the bird or the weapon, and this one brings the weapon back as a sound. Two hundred deaths are heard as two hundred repetitions of the one shot, so that the simile does the accusing that no character has done aloud. The poem will not say where the souls go: they fled to bliss or woe, and the Mariner knows only that they went past him.

quotations.text: Alone, alone, all, all alone, Alone on a wide wide sea! And never a saint took pity on My soul in agony.
quotations.context: The Mariner has just reassured the Wedding-Guest that he is not a ghost, and resumes.
quotations.analysis: The first two lines contain almost nothing but one word and its near-rhymes: 'alone', 'all', 'a'. Long open vowels and the doubled 'wide wide' stretch the line out to the horizon it describes. The loneliness is then made vertical as well as horizontal, since no saint looks down either. He is not literally alone, as the next stanza cruelly points out; he has two hundred companions on deck.

quotations.text: The many men, so beautiful! And they all dead did lie: And a thousand thousand slimy things Lived on; and so did I.
quotations.context: Alone on deck among the bodies of the crew, looking from them to the sea.
quotations.analysis: The men are beautiful only now that they are dead; alive, they were evil looks from old and young. Against them he sets the slimy things and then, after a semicolon that works like a flinch, himself. The grammar files him with the creatures he despises. This self-disgust is the state from which he cannot pray, and the stanza needs to be remembered when the same creatures reappear transformed.

quotations.text: The moving Moon went up the sky, And no where did abide: Softly she was going up, And a star or two beside.
quotations.context: After seven days and nights under the dead men's curse, the Mariner looks up.
quotations.analysis: After stanzas clogged with rot, reek and curses, this one is almost empty, and the change of pace is the change of heart beginning. The moon is 'moving' and the Mariner is stuck; she abides nowhere and yet is accompanied, a star or two beside her, while he is fixed and alone. Nothing is asked of the image. It simply turns his eyes outward, and the water-snakes come two stanzas later.

quotations.text: O happy living things! no tongue Their beauty might declare: A spring of love gushed from my heart, And I blessed them unaware
quotations.context: The Mariner has been watching the water-snakes coil and swim in the shadow of the ship.
quotations.analysis: The turning point of the poem is an action its agent does not know he is performing. 'Unaware' is said twice in the stanza, and it matches the unexplained shooting exactly: he did not decide to kill and he does not decide to bless. 'A spring of love gushed' is water imagery arriving in a drought, and it comes from inside him before any rain falls. Note too that no tongue can declare their beauty, from a man whose whole later life is declaring.

quotations.text: The self same moment I could pray; And from my neck so free The Albatross fell off, and sank Like lead into the sea.
quotations.context: The end of Part IV, immediately after the blessing.
quotations.analysis: Prayer is not the cause of the release but its sign: the blessing came first and was not a prayer at all. The bird, which flew and perched and came to a call, leaves the poem as dead weight, and 'like lead' will be used once more, of the ship itself going down in Part VII. Both burdens sink, and neither sinking ends the matter, which is why this stanza closes a part and not the poem.

quotations.text: They raised their limbs like lifeless tools-- We were a ghastly crew.
quotations.context: The dead sailors rise without speaking and work the ship as it moves without wind.
quotations.analysis: The simile turns the men into the equipment they are handling, and then the pronoun does something worse: 'we'. The Mariner counts himself among them, hauling on a rope beside his own nephew's body. Life-in-Death has won him, and here the phrase is shown from the inside, as a living man doing a shift with corpses and unable to tell himself apart from the gang.

quotations.text: Quoth he, "The man hath penance done, And penance more will do."
quotations.context: The Mariner lies in a faint and hears two voices in the air discussing him; this is the softer one.
quotations.analysis: The sentence is passed in his hearing but not to his face, by speakers who are never identified, and it is the most exact statement of his condition in the poem: penance in the past tense and the future tense, with no present in which it is complete. The soft voice, as soft as honey-dew, delivers the harder news. Everything in Parts VI and VII should be read under this line.

quotations.text: Like one that on a lonesome road Doth walk in fear and dread, And having once turned round walks on, And turns no more his head; Because he knows, a frightful fiend Doth close behind him tread.
quotations.context: The spell of the dead men's eyes has just snapped, and the Mariner looks out over the sea again, but sees little.
quotations.analysis: The simile leaves the sea for a road on land, the place where we first met the Mariner, and describes a man who has looked once and will not look again. The fiend is never seen; knowledge of it is enough. The stanza takes six lines instead of four, so the reader, like the walker, is kept going past the point where rest was expected. Mary Shelley has Frankenstein quote it as he flees his creature.

quotations.text: "Ha! ha!" quoth he, "full plain I see, The Devil knows how to row."
quotations.context: The Pilot has fainted and the Hermit is praying, so the Mariner takes the oars of the rescue boat himself.
quotations.analysis: The boy's joke is the judgement of the ordinary world on the returning Mariner, and it is delivered in laughter by a child who is losing his mind as he speaks. The poem reports his madness in the present tense, in a subordinate clause, as a casualty nobody stops to count. It is a reminder that the tale harms those it touches, which bears on how we read the Wedding-Guest's condition at the end.

quotations.text: Since then, at an uncertain hour, That agony returns; And till my ghastly tale is told, This heart within me burns.
quotations.context: The Mariner has described how the Hermit's question forced the tale out of him, and explains what has happened since.
quotations.analysis: 'Uncertain' removes the last comfort of routine: the penance has no calendar. The burning has moved from the sky and the sea of Part II into his chest, so the tropics are now internal. 'Ghastly' is the word he used of the dead crew at the ropes, and he applies it to his own story. Telling brings relief, which means every listener is being used as medicine, and the Wedding-Guest is only the latest dose.

quotations.text: I pass, like night, from land to land; I have strange power of speech
quotations.context: The Mariner describes his life since the voyage and how he chooses, or is given, his listeners.
quotations.analysis: He compares himself to night, the thing that fell at one stride when the crew died, and the comparison makes him a natural force that arrives everywhere and stays nowhere. 'Strange power of speech' is as close as the poem comes to describing itself. Coleridge, a famous talker who held rooms for hours, gives the gift of eloquence to a man for whom it is a symptom.

quotations.text: He prayeth best, who loveth best All things both great and small; For the dear God who loveth us He made and loveth all.
quotations.context: The Mariner's farewell to the Wedding-Guest.
quotations.analysis: The rhythm goes nursery-simple and the diction could be a hymn for children, which is either the hard-won plainness of a man who has been to the bottom or a formula too small for what it follows. The poem gives grounds for both. The creed says God loves all; the narrative has shown two hundred men killed for a change of opinion. It is worth asking who needs this stanza more, the listener or the speaker.

quotations.text: A sadder and a wiser man, He rose the morrow morn.
quotations.context: The last two lines of the poem; the Mariner has gone, and the Wedding-Guest has turned from the bridegroom's door.
quotations.analysis: The poem ends on the listener, and the order of the adjectives is the verdict: sadder first. The stanza before says he went like one stunned and of sense forlorn, language closer to injury than to enlightenment. He has missed the wedding of his own kin to acquire this wisdom. If the Mariner's moral were the whole meaning, the guest ought to be gladder, and that gap is where the poem's interpretation properly begins.

timeline.label: George Shelvocke's A Voyage Round the World published
timeline.detail: Its account of a rough passage round Cape Horn includes an officer shooting a black albatross in the hope of better weather. Wordsworth later recalled suggesting the incident to Coleridge.

timeline.label: Samuel Taylor Coleridge born at Ottery St Mary, Devon
timeline.detail: The youngest child of the vicar and schoolmaster of the town; he was sent to school at Christ's Hospital in London after his father's death.

timeline.label: Cook's Resolution crosses the Antarctic Circle
timeline.detail: The expedition's astronomer, William Wales, afterwards taught mathematics at Christ's Hospital while Coleridge was a pupil there, a possible route by which descriptions of polar ice reached the poem.

timeline.label: The poem is planned on a November walk in Somerset
timeline.detail: Coleridge, living at Nether Stowey, set out with William and Dorothy Wordsworth from Alfoxden towards the coast. A joint ballad was proposed to pay for the trip, and soon became Coleridge's alone.

timeline.label: Finished in March and published in Lyrical Ballads
timeline.detail: The anonymous volume, printed in Bristol, opened with 'The Rime of the Ancyent Marinere' in deliberately antique spelling, prefaced by a short prose Argument.

timeline.label: Revised for the second edition of Lyrical Ballads
timeline.detail: The spelling was modernised, the title shortened, the poem moved from the front of the volume, and Wordsworth added a note listing what he took to be its defects alongside its merits.

timeline.label: Coleridge moves to Highgate
timeline.detail: He went to live in the household of the surgeon James Gillman, seeking help with his dependence on opium, and stayed for the rest of his life.

timeline.label: Sibylline Leaves adds the marginal gloss
timeline.detail: The poem appeared under Coleridge's name for the first time, with a Latin epigraph from Thomas Burnet and a prose commentary in the margin. Biographia Literaria, with his retrospective account of the Lyrical Ballads plan, came out the same year.

timeline.label: Frankenstein quotes the poem
timeline.detail: Mary Shelley's novel gives Walton an allusion to the albatross and has Victor recite the stanza of the lonesome road, an early sign of the poem's hold on the Gothic imagination.

timeline.label: Final lifetime text; Coleridge dies at Highgate
timeline.detail: The last collected Poetical Works he oversaw prints the version now standard. He died on 25 July.

timeline.label: Gustave Doré's illustrated edition
timeline.detail: Doré's large engravings of the ice, the becalmed ship and the spectre-bark fixed the poem's look for generations of readers.

places.name: Nether Stowey, Somerset
places.note: Coleridge's cottage from the end of 1796, where the poem was written.

places.name: Alfoxden, near Holford
places.note: The house William and Dorothy Wordsworth rented in 1797 and 1798, a few miles' walk from Stowey; the November walk began here.

places.name: Watchet harbour
places.note: The small Bristol Channel port on the route of the 1797 walk, by local tradition the model for the harbour with its kirk, hill and lighthouse. The poem itself names no place.

places.name: Bristol
places.note: Where Joseph Cottle had Lyrical Ballads printed in 1798.

places.name: Cape Horn
places.note: The poem gives no bearings, but a ship driven south to the ice that then runs north into an unvisited sea follows the Horn route of Shelvocke's voyage, and the gloss calls the second sea the Pacific.

places.name: Ottery St Mary, Devon
places.note: Coleridge's birthplace, where his father was vicar.

places.name: Highgate, London
places.note: Coleridge's home from 1816 until his death in 1834, and where the later revisions of the poem were made.

criticalViews.position: The sacramental reading: a coherent parable of sin, penance and grace
criticalViews.summary: On this view the poem means what its Mariner says it means. The killing is a breach of the bond between all living things; the becalming and the deaths are its consequences; the blessing of the water-snakes is an act of love that restores the bond; and the homecoming and the moral complete a pattern of fall and redemption. The gloss of 1817 is Coleridge making that pattern explicit.
criticalViews.counter: It has to pass over the dice game, the wildly unequal punishment of the crew, the Hermit's failure to absolve, and a penance explicitly said to have no end. It also takes the gloss as the poem's own voice, when the gloss is written in a different persona and sometimes asserts what the verse leaves open.

criticalViews.position: The nightmare reading: a universe without reliable justice
criticalViews.summary: Here the poem's power lies in the mismatch between act and consequence. A thoughtless shot brings cosmic retribution; chance decides who lives; spirits pursue their own quarrels; and the pious moral at the end is a frightened man's attempt to make sense of what happened to him. The poem is closer to a bad dream than to a sermon, and its terror is that of guilt felt without a crime understood.
criticalViews.counter: The release in Part IV is too carefully prepared and too exactly mirrors the shooting to be arbitrary, and the Christian imagery is not only in the Mariner's mouth but in the structure of events. To call the moral mere consolation is to decide in advance that the poem cannot mean what it says.

criticalViews.position: The double-text reading: verse and gloss as rival narrators
criticalViews.summary: A third position takes the 1817 page, with ballad in the centre and learned commentary in the margin, as the real work. The gloss names the spirits, assigns motives and draws lessons; the verse does none of these things. The poem thereby stages the act of interpretation itself, and shows a later, tidier mind trying to master an older and wilder story, much as the Mariner's moral tries to master his experience.
criticalViews.counter: For nineteen years the poem existed and was read without any gloss, and it was already strange and already complete. A reading that depends on the margin risks treating an afterthought as the design, and cannot explain the force of the 1798 text.

essayQuestions.question: How far does the Mariner's closing moral account for the poem that precedes it?
essayQuestions.focus: The relation between the stated lesson and the narrated events
plan: Set out the moral exactly: prayer and love of all creatures are one thing, because God made and loves them all. Note its hymn-like simplicity and who speaks it.
Show what it does explain: the hospitality shown to the bird in Part I, its violation, and the unwilled blessing of the water-snakes in Part IV, where love precedes prayer.
Turn to what it leaves out: the dice game in Part III, the deaths of two hundred men for approving an act, and the Pilot's boy driven mad.
Consider the speaker's situation. A man told that more penance is to come, and still seized by agony at uncertain hours, has reasons to want a simple creed.
Conclude with the Wedding-Guest, stunned, forlorn and sadder before he is wiser, as the poem's own evidence that the tale outweighs its moral.

essayQuestions.question: Explore the significance of the Wedding-Guest and the frame in which the tale is told.
essayQuestions.focus: Frame narrative, interruption and the effects of listening
plan: Begin with the opening as an act of selection and restraint: one of three, the hand and then the eye, the guest who cannot choose but hear.
Track the interruptions in Parts I, IV and V, and show that each comes where the tale is most frightening, so the frame regulates the reader's fear.
Set the wedding against the voyage: music, kin and company within earshot of a story about total solitude, and the Mariner's preference for the kirk over the feast.
Use Part VII to show that the frame is also the subject: the origin of the telling in the Hermit's question, and the mechanism of compulsion.
End on the last stanza, which belongs to the guest, and weigh whether the poem presents storytelling as gift, contagion or both.

essayQuestions.question: 'The albatross means whatever the characters need it to mean.' Discuss Coleridge's handling of the bird.
essayQuestions.focus: Symbolism, interpretation and the crew's changing verdicts
plan: Establish what the verse actually shows the bird doing, which is little: arriving, eating, circling, perching, answering a call.
Follow the meanings laid on it in sequence: a Christian soul in simile, the bringer of the breeze, the bringer of the fog, a substitute for the cross, the beloved of a spirit.
Argue that the crew's two sworn verdicts in Part II make interpretation itself a moral act with consequences.
Consider the falling of the bird in Part IV, where it becomes pure weight and sinks like lead, and what is and is not resolved by that.
Relate this to the gloss and to later readings, each of which repeats the crew's gesture of deciding afterwards what the bird was.

essayQuestions.question: How does Coleridge use the ballad form to create a sense of the supernatural?
essayQuestions.focus: Stanza, rhyme, repetition and archaic diction
plan: Describe the inherited form and what it brings with it: speed, impersonality, a teller who does not explain, and an air of age supported by archaic words.
Show internal rhyme and repetition producing both momentum, in the storm and the homecoming, and paralysis, in the becalmed stanzas of Part II.
Examine the stanzas that overrun four lines, such as the portrait of Life-in-Death and the lonesome road, and what the delay of the rhyme does to the reader.
Look at how plainly the uncanny is stated: the shooting, the dead men rising, the ship sinking are each given in the flattest syntax available.
Conclude that the form's refusal to comment is what lets the natural and the supernatural share a single tone, so that neither can be dismissed.

discussionQuestions: The poem never says why the Mariner shot the albatross. Would any reason make the poem better, or is the absence of one the point?
The crew die and the man who fired the shot lives. Is there any account of justice on which that is fair, and does the poem want there to be?
The water-snakes of Part IV are the slimy things of Part II. What has changed, and who or what changed it?
The Hermit is asked for absolution and replies with a question. Is that a failure on his part, or the only honest response available?
Is the Wedding-Guest better off for having heard the tale? What would you need to know about the next morning to decide?
If you read the poem with the 1817 gloss beside it, does the margin help you, or does it seem to be talking about a slightly different poem?

related.why: The 1798 volume the poem opened, where it sits beside Wordsworth's poems of ordinary life and shows how odd a companion it was.
For 'Christabel', 'Kubla Khan' and the conversation poems written in the same Somerset months.
A close reading of the becalmed stanzas of Part II, line by line.
Mary Shelley's novel borrows the poem's frame of a compelled teller and a captive listener, and quotes it twice.
Another voyage in which a single creature is loaded with more meaning than it can settle, told by a sole survivor.
The poem that closed the 1798 Lyrical Ballads, and Wordsworth's very different account of how nature acts on the mind.
